column2: Four months after Pearl Harbor, America bombed Tokyo with just sixteen planes.
The bombs barely scratched the city.
So how did this tiny raid end up changing the entire war in the Pacific?
Simple. It embarrassed Japan so badly that they made the biggest mistake of the war.
In early nineteen forty-two, America was losing everywhere.
Japan had taken the Philippines, Malaya and the Dutch East Indies, and Americans back home wanted revenge.
There was just one problem. Tokyo was way too far away.
Navy planes couldn't fly that far, and Army bombers couldn't take off from a ship.
Until a Navy officer named Francis Low noticed something strange.
Sir, I saw Army bombers practicing on a runway painted like a carrier deck.
So?
What if we put them on a real one?
Bombers are too big to land on a carrier.
They don't land. They just take off.
And then what?
Then they fly to China.
I love it.
And just like that, the craziest plan of the war got approved.
The man chosen to lead it was Jimmy Doolittle, a daredevil racing pilot.
His crews trained to get a heavy bomber off the ground in about five hundred feet.
On April second, the carrier Hornet sailed out of San Francisco with sixteen B twenty-five bombers tied to its deck.
Only at sea did the crews find out where they were going.
Gentlemen, we're going to bomb Tokyo.
Tokyo? Sir, how do we get back?
We don't. We keep flying west and land in China.
Does China know we're coming?
Probably.
The plan was to launch about four hundred and fifty miles from Japan.
As it turned out, the plan did run into a bit of a problem.
At dawn on April eighteenth, a small Japanese patrol boat spotted the fleet, still six hundred and fifty miles out.
It was sunk within minutes, but it had already radioed Tokyo.
Launch the bombers. Now.
Sir, that's two hundred extra miles. We won't have the fuel to reach China.
Then fly carefully.
One by one, all sixteen bombers roared off the pitching deck. Not a single one fell into the sea.
Around noon, they hit Tokyo, Yokohama, Nagoya, Kobe and Osaka.
The damage was small, but for Japan, the shock was enormous.
Enemy bombers over the Emperor's capital? That was supposed to be impossible.
Then night fell, and the fuel ran out.
Fifteen planes crash-landed or were abandoned over China. One landed in the Soviet Union.
Doolittle sat next to his wrecked bomber, sure he would be court-martialed.
I lost every single plane.
Instead, he got the Medal of Honor, and a promotion to general.
China paid the real price. In revenge, Japanese troops killed an estimated two hundred and fifty thousand civilians.
And in Tokyo, Admiral Yamamoto was furious.
To make sure this never happened again, he pushed through his plan to attack Midway Island.
Seven weeks later, at Midway, Japan lost four aircraft carriers in a single battle.
Sixteen bombers that barely hit anything had just triggered the turning point of the Pacific War.
